content: The hygiene hypothesis in medicine posits that insufficient exposure to infectious agents during early childhood, and later a lack of exposure to helminths in adulthood, increases the likelihood of developing allergic diseases. This hypothesis was first introduced by David P. Strachan in a 1989 article published in the British Medical Journal (now BMJ). It was formulated to explain the observation that allergic conditions such as hay fever and eczema were less prevalent in children from larger families. These children were presumed to have greater exposure to infectious agents through their siblings compared to children from smaller families or single-child households. The hygiene hypothesis has been extensively studied by immunologists and epidemiologists and has become a significant theoretical framework for understanding allergic disorders. However, the specific infectious microorganisms or their components responsible for these effects have not yet been identified or integrated into medical practice. Additionally, the role of hygiene levels in the increasing prevalence of allergic diseases remains unproven. Allergic diseases arise from inappropriate immune responses to harmless antigens, driven by an overactive TH2-type immune response. Many bacteria and viruses, on the other hand, elicit a TH1-type immune response, which can suppress the mediators of TH2 responses. Early observations of immune function led to the initial mechanism proposed under the hygiene hypothesis: insufficient stimulation of the TH1 arm of the immune system results in an overactive TH2 arm, which in turn leads to allergic diseases. However, this explanation fell out of favor because it could not account for the simultaneous rise in autoimmune diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), multiple sclerosis (MS), and type 1 diabetes, which are associated with an overactive TH1 response, in the same populations experiencing increased allergic diseases. An alternative mechanism was later proposed to address this limitation. It suggests that the developing immune system, if not exposed to infectious agents, fails to properly develop regulatory cells. A deficiency in these regulatory cells predisposes individuals to autoimmune diseases due to poorly controlled TH1 reactions and to allergic diseases due to poorly controlled TH2 reactions. To use an analogy, an unregulated immune system behaves like an unruly, unsupervised party, prone to overreacting to minor or nonexistent threats and even attacking the body’s own cells. Regulatory T cells act as the immune system’s bouncers, requiring practice to become robust and effective. The old friends hypothesis refines the hygiene hypothesis further. It posits that regulatory T cells can only become fully functional when stimulated by exposure to specific microorganisms and parasites. These include pathogens with low levels of pathogenicity that have coexisted universally with humans throughout evolutionary history—until recently, when hygienic practices and modern medical care have reduced or eliminated these organisms from human populations. For example, the proper development of regulatory T cells may depend on exposure to organisms such as lactobacilli, various mycobacteria, and even certain harmless helminths. These regulatory cells learn to modulate the immune system’s response to harmless or beneficial invaders, preventing aggressive reactions from helper T cells and other immune components to antigens presented by these benign symbionts. Consequently, a well-developed immune system is less likely to attack harmless allergens or the body’s own cells. In this context, both overly virulent and excessively sterile environments are detrimental to optimal immune system development. Recent research has revealed even more striking benefits for individuals with conditions such as multiple sclerosis and Crohn’s disease. The reasoning is that our immune systems evolved under constant exposure to a variety of parasites, many of which modulate the immune response to ensure their survival. These parasites downregulate the immune response that would otherwise target them. Without these downregulating parasites, our immune systems, which evolved to function in their presence, often attack our own tissues. This leads to conditions such as asthma, hay fever, IBD, colitis, Crohn’s disease, multiple sclerosis, and potentially other autoimmune diseases. This explains the rise in autoimmune diseases in the relatively clean and sterile environments of industrialized societies.
